opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what we actually want these systems to understand. Much of the recent progress in AI has come from language, and language is an incredibly powerful compression of human knowledge. But it's still a compression. It's something humans wrote *about* the world after experiencing it. If you only learn from that, you're learning from a secondhand description, and a lot of what matters about the physical world never gets written down at all.

Think about how a child learns. Before they can say a single word, they already have a sense of object permanence, of gravity, of what happens when you push something off a table. Nobody taught them that through text. They learned it by looking, touching, moving around, and seeing the consequences. That kind of grounded, embodied, predictive understanding is what I think a real world model needs to have.

There's also a deeper issue. If you train only on internet data, including internet videos, you're mostly learning from a curated, edited, human-filtered slice of reality. Videos get cut. The camera points at the interesting part. The boring but physically important continuity often gets lost. A model can produce something that looks very convincing and still fail to understand why things happen. It learns appearance more than causality.

So when I say world models need the real world, I mean they need contact with the actual dynamics of reality: continuous sensory streams, the ability to act and observe what changes, and the kind of messy, long-tail situations you can't fake. That's where you find out whether a model truly understands something or is just pattern-matching on what it's seen before.

Simulation helps, and generated data helps, but ultimately the real world is the ground truth. It's the only environment that doesn't share our blind spots. If we want intelligence that can operate in the physical world, in robotics, in spatial reasoning, in everyday life, then at some point it has to learn from the world itself, not just from our descriptions of it.

r001.rationale: The response argues for learning physical dynamics to support robotics and everyday operation, but does not clearly ground the problems world models address in human needs.

r002.rationale: It says internet data and videos are insufficient and that models must ultimately learn from the real world itself, including dynamics and situations that cannot be faked.

r003.rationale: It describes internet videos as curated and human-filtered, but does not identify YouTube or clearly describe YouTube’s data distribution.

r004.rationale: It emphasizes embodied learning through touching and acting, and says models need continuous sensory streams and the ability to act and observe, communicating the importance of non-visual experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that a world model, by definition, is a model of the world, and the world is not made of text, and it's not made of internet video either. Those are projections of the world, filtered through what humans chose to write down or point a camera at.

If you train only on language, you get something that's very good at reasoning about descriptions of the world. That's valuable, but there's a gap between knowing that a glass will shatter if you drop it and actually having a representation of how objects fall, how surfaces reflect light, how a scene changes when you move your head three centimeters to the left. Language skips most of that because humans never bothered to say it. It's the stuff we take for granted.

Internet video closes some of that gap, and I'm actually quite optimistic about scaling visual self-supervised learning on web-scale data. But web video is still a biased, curated slice. It's mostly things people found interesting enough to upload. It's third-person, it's edited, and there's almost no feedback loop. The model watches, but it never acts and sees what happens as a consequence of its own action.

That last part is what I mean by needing the real world. A world model should let you ask counterfactual questions: if I do this, what happens next? To learn that well, I think at some point you need data where the agent's actions are actually in the loop, whether that comes from robots, from embodied agents, or from people interacting with systems in physical space. Otherwise you're learning correlation in a passive stream, and you end up with a very good video predictor that doesn't understand causality.

So my view is less "the internet is useless" and more that the internet gives you a strong prior, and the real world gives you grounding and correction. The interesting research question right now is how to combine the two, so that the expensive real-world data corrects the cheap large-scale data instead of being drowned out by it.

r001.rationale: The response advocates grounding models in physical interaction and real-world feedback, but does not connect that grounding to human needs.

r002.rationale: It says that, at some point, training needs data with an agent’s actions in the loop, which passive internet video does not provide.

r003.rationale: It describes web video as a biased, curated slice made up mostly of things people found interesting enough to upload, conveying the skew toward human interests.

r004.rationale: It discusses language, video, and physical interaction, but does not state that non-visual data is crucial for training world models.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what does it mean to understand the world? A model can watch a lot of videos and become very good at predicting what the next frame should look like. But that doesn’t necessarily mean it understands what will happen if it takes an action.

Imagine a cup sitting on a table. From images, you can learn what a cup looks like and where it usually appears. But if you push it, will it slide, tip over, or stay in place? That depends on properties that may not be visible—its weight, the friction, whether it’s full. You learn about those properties through interaction, by making predictions and getting feedback.

So when I say world models need the real world, I mean they need that connection between observation, action, and consequence. Video and simulation can be incredibly useful. But ultimately, we need to test whether what the model has learned actually supports acting in the world. Can it anticipate the consequences of an action? Can it recognize when it’s uncertain and gather more information? Can it update when reality surprises it? To me, that feedback loop is central.

r001.rationale: The response argues that world models need action and consequence feedback from the real world, but does not connect their problems to real-world human needs.

r002.rationale: It discusses real-world feedback, but does not state that training requires real-world data unavailable on the internet.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention YouTube or a data distribution skewed toward human interests.

r004.rationale: It notes that some physical properties are not visible and can be learned through interaction, but does not state that non-visual data is crucial for training world models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that a world model needs to learn what happens when you act, not just what the world looks like. You can watch a lot of video and learn very strong patterns, but watching alone doesn’t necessarily tell you what would happen if you intervened—if you pushed an object differently, or tried something you hadn’t seen before.

The real world gives you that feedback. You make a prediction, take an action, and discover whether your understanding was right. And often the most useful information is precisely where you were wrong.

That doesn’t mean all training has to happen in the physical world. Simulation and recorded data can be incredibly useful. But ultimately, if we want these models to operate in the real world, reality has to be the thing that tests and corrects them.

r001.rationale: The response says models need real-world feedback to learn from actions, but does not connect their problems to real-world human needs.

r002.rationale: It says reality must ultimately test and correct models, but does not state that training requires data unavailable on the internet.
